title: WHY DID ADONIJAH WANT ABISHAG? THE MARRIAGE REQUEST THAT GOT A PRINCE KILLED
paragraphs: WHY DID ADONIJAH WANT ABISHAG? THE MARRIAGE REQUEST THAT GOT A PRINCE KILLED

He asked for one woman. Solomon heard a claim to a kingdom. And hidden inside this disturbing story is a warning for every person who has ever surrendered to God with their mouth while secretly reaching back for the throne.
There are requests in the Bible that sound harmless until you understand what they actually mean.
Adonijah’s request for Abishag is one of them.
At first glance, the story can seem almost brutally unfair.
A prince wants to marry a beautiful woman.
He asks Bathsheba to speak to King Solomon on his behalf.
Bathsheba delivers the request.
Solomon hears it.
And suddenly a man is dead.
What happened?
Why would asking for a wife provoke a royal execution?
And perhaps the more uncomfortable question is this:
Was Adonijah really asking only for Abishag?
Because once you read the story in its political, biblical, and spiritual context, something chilling begins to emerge.
Adonijah had already tried to become king.
He had already reached for a throne God had given to someone else.
He had already been spared.
And now, after receiving mercy, he reached toward something intimately associated with the previous king.
That changes everything.

Before David died, Scripture introduces Abishag the Shunammite during the final weakness of his old age. David could no longer keep himself warm, so his servants searched Israel for a young woman who could attend him.
The Hebrew of 1 Kings 1:3–4 says:
“וַיְבַקְשׁוּ נַעֲרָה יָפָה בְּכֹל גְּבוּל יִשְׂרָאֵל וַיִּמְצְאוּ אֶת־אֲבִישַׁג הַשּׁוּנַמִּית... וְהַנַּעֲרָה יָפָה עַד־מְאֹד... וְהַמֶּלֶךְ לֹא יְדָעָהּ”
They searched throughout Israel for a beautiful young woman and found Abishag the Shunammite. She became David’s attendant and served him, but, literally, “the king did not know her.”
That last phrase matters.

In biblical Hebrew, “to know” can function as a discreet expression for sexual relations. The narrative therefore deliberately tells us that although Abishag occupied an extraordinarily intimate position beside David, David did not have sexual relations with her.
Then comes one of the most important transitions in the story.
Immediately after introducing David’s weakness and Abishag’s presence, Scripture says of Adonijah:
“אֲנִי אֶמְלֹךְ”
“I will be king.”
There is the heart of the crisis.
Adonijah was not merely another son of David living quietly in Jerusalem.
He had already exalted himself as David’s successor.
He gathered chariots.
Horsemen.
Fifty men running before him.
He secured powerful supporters.
He arranged a sacrificial feast.
He invited royal sons and influential leaders.
And he positioned himself as though the crown were already his.
But the kingdom was not his to take.
David publicly installed Solomon as king.
Adonijah’s attempted accession collapsed.
Terrified, Adonijah fled to the altar and grasped its horns.
Solomon could have immediately treated him as an enemy.
Instead, Solomon showed him mercy.
That detail is crucial.
Adonijah was given another morning.
Another opportunity.
Another chance to walk away from his ambition.
Solomon essentially placed his future in his own hands: if he proved himself worthy, he could live; if wickedness were found in him, he would die.
Then David died.
Solomon’s throne became established.
And Adonijah approached Bathsheba.
David’s widow.
Solomon’s mother.
“Do you come peaceably?” she asked.
He answered that he did.
Then he said something revealing.
He reminded her that the kingdom had once been expected to become his.
He even acknowledged that it had turned and become Solomon’s “from the LORD.”
Read that carefully.
Adonijah knew.
At least verbally, he acknowledged God’s providence.
He knew Solomon possessed the throne.
He knew the kingdom had come to Solomon from Yahweh.
And yet his next request reached straight back into David’s royal household.
He asked Bathsheba:
Please ask King Solomon to give me Abishag the Shunammite as my wife.
One woman.
One marriage.
One apparently modest request.
Solomon heard something much larger.
His response was explosive:
Why ask Abishag for Adonijah?
Why not ask the kingdom for him also?
That sentence is the interpretive key to the entire episode.
Solomon himself connects the request for Abishag with a request for the kingdom.
This is where we must be careful not to claim more than Scripture says.
The Bible never gives us a sentence saying, “Adonijah requested Abishag because he planned to use the marriage to overthrow Solomon.”
We cannot read his private thoughts.
Perhaps Abishag’s extraordinary beauty genuinely attracted him. Scripture had explicitly described her as exceedingly beautiful.
But Solomon did not regard the request as an innocent romantic proposal.
And there was a serious reason.
In the world of Israel’s monarchy, possession of a king’s women could carry dynastic and political meaning.
We have already seen something similar in the story of Saul.
When Ish-bosheth accused Abner concerning Rizpah, Saul’s concubine, the accusation immediately detonated into a political confrontation involving royal loyalty and the transfer of the kingdom.
Later, Absalom publicly went in to David’s concubines after seizing Jerusalem.
This was not merely sexual immorality performed in private.
It was a public political declaration.
David’s household was being treated as belonging to the man presenting himself as David’s replacement.

So when Adonijah—the former rival claimant to David’s throne—asked for the woman who had occupied an intimate place in David’s final royal household, Solomon interpreted it against that larger royal background.
Later Jewish tradition likewise recognized Abishag’s association with royal status. The Talmud preserves a discussion portraying her as connected to the prerogatives of kingship.
Again, we should not confuse later rabbinic interpretation with the inspired biblical text itself.
But it demonstrates how strongly Abishag could be understood as belonging to the symbolic world of Davidic royalty.
And suddenly Solomon’s reaction becomes far less mysterious.
Adonijah was not simply some unknown young man asking to marry some unrelated young woman.
He was the man who had already said:
“I will be king.”
He had already attempted to occupy Solomon’s throne.
He had already received mercy.
He had already acknowledged that Solomon’s kingdom was from the LORD.
And now he was requesting the woman associated with David’s final royal household.
Solomon heard an echo of the throne.
And this is where an ancient royal scandal becomes frighteningly personal.
Because Adonijah’s tragedy was not merely that he wanted something.
It was that grace had given him an opportunity to become a different man, yet the old hunger still appears in the story.
How many of us understand that?
We surrender something to God...
and then quietly negotiate for a smaller version of it.
We say we have surrendered our pride, but still desperately need recognition.
We say we have surrendered lust, but preserve one secret doorway.
We say we have forgiven, but continue rehearsing the offense because anger still gives us something.
We say Jesus is Lord, but there remains one chair in the hidden room of the heart where we still insist on sitting.
Adonijah had lost the throne.
But now he wanted something Solomon understood as connected to the throne.
That is the terrifying anatomy of unsurrendered desire.
Sometimes sin stops demanding the whole kingdom.
Sometimes it only asks for Abishag.
Just one compromise.
One private message.
One hidden relationship.
One secret habit.
One little bitterness.
One quiet fantasy.
One untouched corner of your life.
Nothing dramatic.
Nothing that looks like rebellion.
Just...
this one thing.
But God sees where the road goes.
There are things we call “small” because we are looking at the request.
God is looking at the throne behind the request.
And that should make every believer examine the heart.
What are you still negotiating with God about?
What have you technically surrendered while emotionally keeping the key?
What did grace rescue you from that you have slowly begun approaching again?
This story becomes even more serious when we remember that Adonijah had already experienced mercy.
Solomon had spared him.
Grace had interrupted judgment.
But mercy is not permission to return to rebellion.
The New Testament expresses the principle with unmistakable clarity:
“Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid.”
Grace is not God pretending rebellion does not matter.
Grace is God opening the door for rebels to become sons and daughters.
And this is where we must go beyond Solomon.
Because Solomon can expose something about judgment, kingship, and the seriousness of rebellion.
But Solomon cannot save us.
Another Son of David would eventually come.
Jesus Christ.
And unlike Adonijah, Jesus never seized a throne that did not belong to Him.
He humbled Himself.
He obeyed the Father.
He went willingly toward the cross.
And there, the rightful King allowed rebels to mock Him as king.
They placed a crown of thorns on His head.
They dressed Him in mock royalty.
They struck Him.
They crucified Him.
And above Him they placed the accusation:
King of the Jews.
Think about the scandal.
Human beings have spent our lives trying to occupy God’s throne...
and God the Son came down from glory to save the very rebels who wanted His place.
That is the Gospel.
We were not innocent victims needing motivational advice.
We were sinners needing reconciliation.
We had loved ourselves.
Protected ourselves.
Exalted ourselves.
Hidden ourselves.
Justified ourselves.
We wanted forgiveness without surrender.
Heaven without holiness.
Jesus as Savior without Jesus as Lord.
We wanted the benefits of His kingdom while remaining rulers of our own.
Yet Christ died for sinners.
He rose again.
And now He does something far greater than merely canceling punishment.
He makes people new.
This is why repentance is beautiful.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is God liberating you from the exhausting delusion that you were ever meant to be king.
You can finally get off the throne.
You can stop pretending.
Stop hiding.
Stop protecting the secret.
Stop negotiating.
Stop telling Jesus, “Everything is Yours... except this.”
Maybe your Abishag has a name.
Maybe nobody knows it.
Maybe it is not sexual sin at all.
Maybe it is approval.
Money.
Control.
Resentment.
Jealousy.
Status.
A relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
A wound you have turned into an identity.
A private addiction.
A public image.
A dream you would rather possess without God than surrender to God.
And perhaps the Holy Spirit has been touching that exact place while you have been reading.
Do not run from conviction.
Run to Christ.
There is a difference between condemnation and conviction.
Condemnation whispers that there is no road home.
The Gospel announces that the road home has a name.
Jesus.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Not some unrighteousness.
All.
This is why the cross is simultaneously devastating and beautiful.
At Calvary, God does not tell us our sin was insignificant.
He shows us how serious it was.
And then He shows us how enormous His mercy is.
Your scandal does not have to write your final chapter.
Peter’s denial did not.
Paul’s persecution of Christians did not.
The Samaritan woman’s broken history did not.
The thief’s criminal past did not.
And if you come to Christ in repentance and faith, yours does not have to either.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe that is exactly why you encountered this article.
Not merely to learn why an ancient prince wanted an ancient woman.
But to discover what your own heart has been reaching for.
Adonijah’s story forces an uncomfortable question:
After mercy spared you, what did you reach for next?
Do not answer that publicly unless you should.
But answer it before God.
Be honest.
Because the most dangerous throne may not be sitting inside a palace.
It may be sitting inside the human heart.
And there is only one King worthy of it.
Jesus Christ.
Someone reading silently may desperately need evidence that Jesus still restores broken people.
Not because every sentence is equally important, but because there may come a night when the thing you surrendered starts calling your name again.
Send it to the believer who looks strong publicly but may be exhausted privately. Share it with the skeptic who thinks Christianity is merely about respectable people behaving better.
Show them the scandal.
Then show them the grace.
Salvation cannot be purchased, and financially supporting a ministry is never a condition for glorifying God.
We glorify God through Christ-centered faith, obedience, worship, generosity, love, and faithful stewardship.
Your support helps us keep producing Christ-centered teaching, Scripture-based encouragement, discipleship material, and resources designed to point people back to Jesus.
Because somewhere tonight, someone is still reaching for the very thing God rescued them from.
Maybe they need this story.
Maybe you did too.
And remember this:
The throne you finally surrender may become the place where grace finally begins rebuilding you.
